holding_summary: The court held that letting out furnished rooms to gentlemen for pay as a boarding house was the tenant's assumed lawful and ordinary purpose in hiring the house, and that the landlord's alleged knowledge of the house's prior disreputable use and false representation that it was 'a good place' for that business raised a jury question of fraudulent concealment, rather than a matter properly decided against the tenant as a matter of law.

quotes.text: It is a subject of defense and recoupment, in an action for rent, that premises demised for the purpose of keeping a respectable boarding house therein had beén previously occupied, to the knowledge of the lessor, without disclosing it, as a house-Of ill-fatn'e, and continued, after such demise, in consequence thereof, tobe subject to nightly visits at all hours, from disreputable persons of both sexes, to the .annoyance and disturbance of the tenant, and bringing, reproach and disgrace upon herself and her family, thus defeating the purposes and uses for which she rént'ed tbe bouse, and forcing her to abandon her business therein.
The evidence in the present case tended to show that the plaintiff represented that the premises were “a good place” for the defendant to let out rooms furnished to gentlemen.

The question of fact as to the character of the house at the time of the letting being known to the plaintiff, and his false representation or fraudulent concealment thereof from the defendant, we think should have been submitted to the jury.

holding_summary: In an action for rent under leases of two houses hired to be operated as a boarding house, the court held that even if a covenant is implied that leased premises are fit for occupation as a boarding house, that implied covenant does not extend by implication to fitness for a 'first class' or any other particular description of boarding house not expressly stated in the lease, and affirmed judgment for the landlords where no fraud or misrepresentation as to nearby nuisances was proven.

quotes.text: Even if a covenant can be implied in a lease of promises to be used as a “ boarding house,” that when let they are suitable for occupation as a “ boarding house,” such a covenant cannot be extended, by implication, to “ first’class,” or any particular description of boarding house not expressly designated in the lease.

The actions were brought upon leases dated March 18th, 1861, made by the plaintiffs as landlords, to the defendant as tenant of two adjoining houses, Nos. 1 and 3 East 20th street, for the rent which remained unpaid up to the time of trial.

Conceding that there is an implied covenant in the lease that the premises when let, were fit and suitable for occupation as boarding houses, such covenant cannot be so extended by implication as to cover first class, or any particular description of boarding houses not expressly designated in the lease.

quotes.text: the defendant Cushing during all this time kept a boarding-house, and that the defendant Green boarded with her
It follows therefore that the justice was right in giving judgment in favor of the defendant Cushing under her lien as a boarding-house keeper.

The chattel mortgage given the plaintiff by the defendant Green, not having been recorded until after all the indebtedness claimed by the defendant Cushing in this action accrued, was not a valid lien upon the furniture as against the defendant Cushing’s claim under the boarding-house keepers’ act.

holding_summary: In a libel action by a woman who kept a respectable boarding house for several years, the court held that a newspaper's publication calling her house home to a 'blackmailing crowd' was libelous per se, treating good character and respectability as valuable assets of her boarding-house business, though the judgment was reversed for improper admission of unrelated evidence.

quotes.text: The evidence shows that the plaintiff was a person of good character, and keeping a large and respectable boardinghouse, which was a source of income and support for herself and her children, and that the publication complained of caused her injury, and damaged her business. Good character and respectability are elements of value in every worthy pursuit in life, and probably in few more so, than in the business conducted by the plaintiff.
The conclusion reached in Edsall v. Brooks (2 Robt. 34), “that the term ‘ blackmailing ’ is universally regarded as an unlawful act,” and is libelous per se, is one to be concurred in.
